To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the diffraction from the ice can be removed from the diffraction of the crystal, and the resulting diffraction data can be used for phasing and refinement.
ice diffraction can be subtracted from diffraction data, and that this leads to a significant increase in the completeness of the data.
ice ring subtraction can be applied successfully to macromolecular crystal data and can improve the quality of the final model.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of new methods and algorithms for the analysis of macromolecular crystallographic data, in particular, the processing of data obtained at synchrotron beamlines and the determination of structures of macromolecules in complex with ligands and in solution.
the development of methods to improve the quality of macromolecular diffractions, particularly in the presence of the ice rings that are commonly observed in cryocooled samples.
the recovery of diffraction intensity in the presence of strong ice rings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best diffraction data is obtained when the sample is not cryoprotected, and that cryoprotecting the sample leads to a reduction in the diffraction quality.
the ice rings are best removed by the use of cryoprotective reagents that minimize the ice ring problem, but that the approach of de-icing can be used to advantage when this is not possible.
, if the crystal is sufficiently stable, it is possible to obtain useful data in the presence of a significant amount of ice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best data quality for cryocrystallography is obtained with the least possible level of cryoprotective agent.
the best results are obtained by optimizing the cryoprotectation, but that the ice rings can be removed in a straightforward manner when necessary.
the ice ring subtraction is not the panacea to solve all cryo-crystallographic problems, but it is a useful addition to the arsenal of techniques for dealing with cryo-crystals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the presence of strong ice rings, the data quality is not necessarily improved by excluding the affected data.
the ice rings can be removed from the diffraction data, allowing for a more complete data set and, in turn, improved phasing.
, when ice diffraction is present in the data, the diffraction of the macromolecule can still be recovered.
